note: Words that set the scene and change nothing in the game: the title page, the card that opens each season, and the chronicle's opening and closing lines. The UI picks a line from what is true in the city, by a hash of the seed and the season, never with the game's dice, so a replay stays exact. All lines are invention unless tagged history. Conditions: grainLow (under 3 months), carthageNear (clock 7 or more), plotNamed (a known plot has a name), plotKnown (any warned plot), guardUnpaid, tyranny (you hold citadel, generalship and treasury), quiet (no warned plot and no rival).

title.name: Heloris on tyranny
title.by: Heloris, to Dionysius, as Diodorus tells it (14.8.5)

title.name: ΣΥΡΑΚΟΣΙΩΝ on the coins
title.by: "Of the Syracusans", as struck on the city's silver in these years
title.source: ANS 2015.1.1, tetradrachm of Syracuse, 405 to 400 BC

seasons.text: The vintage is in. Ploughs go out to the wet fields and the seed goes down behind them.
The last merchantmen of the year crowd the Great Harbour before the seas close.
Must ferments in the jars. Every tavern in Achradina has an opinion about you.
Rain on the Island. Ships stay hauled up, and men have time to talk.
The olive presses creak through the short days. Smoke hangs over the roofs at dusk.
North wind across Epipolae. The watch on the walls stamps its feet and counts the hours.
The seas open. Sails on the horizon could be grain, or envoys, or worse.
The barley ripens on the plain of the Anapus. Young men drill in the agora.
Swallows over the spring of Arethusa. Everyone is suddenly busy, and everyone is watching.
Threshing floors ring with flails. Dust and chaff blow down to the harbour.
Cicadas in the olive groves. The heat keeps the streets empty at noon and the dinners late.
The campaigning season. Somewhere, men are sharpening bronze.
Bread is dear. Mothers queue at the granaries before dawn and go home with half a measure.
The bakers' ovens in Achradina stand cold. Hungry cities remember who fed them.
Fishermen swear they saw purple sails off Plemmyrium. Carthage is stirring.
Traders from the west say the Punic yards are busy day and night.
You know a name now. You see it in every face that smiles at you.
You sleep in a different room each night. The hair above you is very thin.
Conversations stop when you enter. Something is being arranged without you.
Your food is tasted twice. Your watchers bring you scraps of talk and no names.
The guard counts what it is owed, out loud, where you can hear.
Citadel, treasury, command: all in one hand. The city calls it peace. It is quiet, which is not the same.
Men bow lower than they used to. You cannot tell any more what they think.
A calm season, as far as anyone can see. In Syracuse that is never very far.
No whispers reach you. Either all is well, or your watchers are not watching.

chronicle.text: Here is set down what was done at Syracuse under Dionysius, season by season, as it was seen from the Island.
Here the chronicle ends, as he did.
Here the chronicle ends. The sword still hangs; it has not yet fallen.
Here the chronicle of this reign ends.
